125	|---|---|---|---|
126	| 2022 (from 15 Mar) | 1,010 | 505 | 541 |
127	| 2023 | 602 | 301 | 397 |
128	| 2024 | 1,004 | 502 | 542 |
129	| 2025 | 1,022 | 511 | 740 |
130	| 2026 (to 7 Sep) | 503 | 448 | 405 |
131	| **Total** | 4,141 | **2,267** | |
132	
133	Duration: median 38 min, 95th percentile 231 min, maximum 673 min. No overlapping intervals. 10 alerts are shorter than 2 min; 29 pairs of alerts are less than 5 min apart (not merged, decision 5).
134	
135	## Exploratory analysis
136	
137	Done on a 1-minute grid (2.36M points, 2022-03-15 … 2026-09-07) with [scripts/eda.py](scripts/eda.py); the full numeric output is in [reports/eda_output.txt](reports/eda_output.txt). "Recent" below means from 2025-07-01. The analysis was run to answer six questions that the plan depended on.
138	
139	### 1. Do neighbours predict Kyiv, and how early?
140	
141	Yes. The strongest signal is Kyiv oblast: when it is under alert and the city is not, a city alert starts within 30 min in 12.5% of cases against a 3.5% base rate (recent).
142	
143	- In 63% of city alert starts Kyiv oblast was already under alert; in 51% for at least 10 min, in 35% for at least 30 min; the median is 36 min.
144	- 37% of city alerts start with no alert in Kyiv oblast — these cannot be caught from neighbours.
145	
146	The 30-minute horizon is kept: it matches the typical lead.
147	
148	![Lead time](reports/figures/lead_time.png)
149	
150	### 2. Which regions count as neighbours?
151	
152	| Region | Share of time under alert | Precision | Lift | Recall |
153	|---|---|---|---|---|
154	| Kyiv oblast | 13% | 12.5% | 3.6× | 47% |
155	| Cherkasy | 8% | 11.0% | 3.1× | 26% |
156	| Zhytomyr | 5% | 8.7% | 2.5× | 13% |
157	| Poltava | 28% | 6.0% | 1.7× | 48% |
158	| Chernihiv | 60% | 4.7% | 1.3× | 81% |
159	| Sumy | 76% | 3.9% | 1.1× | 83% |
160	| Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk | 92–100% | ≈3.5% | 1.0× | 93–100% |
161	
162	Recent period, Kyiv city quiet. Precision = P(city alert starts within 30 min | region under alert); recall = share of pre-alert minutes covered by the signal. Lift = precision divided by the 3.5% base rate.
163	
164	Recall alone is misleading here: Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk reach 93–100% only because they are under alert almost all the time. Their lift of 1.0 means that knowing their state does not change the odds for Kyiv at all. They are kept as features anyway (decision 16).
165	
166	Chernihiv, the motivating example of this project, gives 4.7% against a 3.5% base rate as a plain yes/no flag, because it is under alert most of the time. Western oblasts (Chernivtsi 12%, Vinnytsia 10%) are precise but rare: they switch on only during nationwide alerts, recall 2–6%. This is the reason for decision 13.
167	
168	![Neighbour signal](reports/figures/neighbour_signal.png)
169	
170	### 3. Did the move to raion-level alerts break the oblast flag?
171	
172	Partly.
173	
174	- Kyiv oblast: the share of time under alert jumped from 5.6% to 22.6% in the second half of 2024, while all its rows were still oblast-level. This is a real increase in attacks, not an aggregation effect. After the move to raions (2025) it stays at 17–26%.
175	- Chernihiv: here the effect is real — 28% → 55% → 68% right after the move.
176	- Kharkiv: 100% of the time from mid-2024 because of a single hromada-level alert that lasted 604 days.
177	
178	![Share of time under alert](reports/figures/alert_share_heatmap.png)
179	
180	### 4. Is it worth training on 2022–2023?
181	
182	The data drifts:
183	
184	- 2023 is the quietest year (301 alerts, 4.6% of the time under alert).
185	- Median duration falls: 49 → 55 → 34 → 35 → 30 min (2022 → 2026).
186	- Share of alerts starting at night (22:00–06:00 Kyiv time): 31% in 2022, 48% in 2025, 39% in 2026.
187	- After 2 hours of alert the chance to end within 30 min was 36% in 2022–2024 and 22% in 2025–2026.
188	
189	Analysis alone cannot settle this, hence decision 14.
190	
191	![Kyiv alerts per month](reports/figures/kyiv_alerts_per_month.png)
192	![Start hour by year](reports/figures/kyiv_start_hour_by_year.png)
193	![End curve](reports/figures/kyiv_end_curve.png)
194	
195	### 5. How rare is the event?
196	
197	- "Start" task: 3.0% of quiet minutes are followed by an alert within 30 min. This is the PR-AUC of random guessing.
198	- "End" task: 37% of alert minutes are followed by an end within 30 min.
199	
200	With the split planned before EDA:
201	
202	| Part | Kyiv alert starts | "Start" base rate |
203	|---|---|---|
204	| Train (to March 2026) | 1,957 | 2.9% |
205	| Validation (April–June 2026) | 139 | 3.3% |
206	| Test (July – 6 September 2026) | 171 | 5.5% |
207	
208	The test period is about twice as intense as training: August 2026 had 90 alerts, the most since March 2022. Validation is small, so a threshold picked on 139 events would be noisy — this led to decision 15.
209	
210	### 6. Data quality across all regions
211	
212	- 2 rows with zero duration (Odesa and Kharkiv oblasts, November 2025) — dropped by the loader, 185,428 rows remain.
213	- 451 rows shorter than 1 min; 897 longer than 24 h, almost all in Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
214	- Overlapping intervals within the same raion or hromada: 0.
215	- Luhansk: 1 row; its permanent alert is not in the data, so the region is excluded.
216	
217	## Time
218	
219	The dataset is in UTC with a constant offset all year. Checked against known events: the mass strike of 2022-10-10 starts at 03:47 in the data, which is 06:47 Kyiv summer time.
220	
221	The problem: Ukraine switches between UTC+2 (winter) and UTC+3 (summer), so the same UTC hour is a different hour for people. The data shows it: the peak of alert starts in Kyiv moves from 21:00 UTC in summer to 22:00–23:00 UTC in winter, while in Kyiv time it stays around midnight (2024–2026, small sample).
222	
223	Options considered:
224	
225	| Option | Idea | Verdict |
226	|---|---|---|
227	| **A** | Computations in UTC, calendar features in `Europe/Kyiv` | **chosen** |
228	| B | Convert the whole dataset to Kyiv time | The autumn hour 03:00–04:00 occurs twice, the spring one does not exist; an offset would have to be stored next to every timestamp |
229	| C | Everything in UTC + a "summer time" feature | Baselines cannot learn the shift, so the model comparison becomes unfair |
230	| D | Fixed offset all year | The hour is off by one for half of the year |
231	
232	How A works: the time grid, region states, durations, lags and the target are computed in UTC, where a day is always 24 hours. For each grid point the Kyiv hour and day of week are computed separately with `zoneinfo`. On a switch night the grid stays regular; in autumn two neighbouring hours simply get the same label, and in spring one label is skipped.
233	
234	No Kyiv alert in the dataset spans a switch moment (checked on all 9 switches); other oblasts were not checked.
235	
236	## Evaluation
237	
238	**Metrics**
239	
240	- PR-AUC — primary (classes are imbalanced).
241	- Brier score and calibration curve.
242	- Precision / recall / F1 at a threshold picked on validation; the yes / no answer comes from this threshold.
243	- Number of false "yes" per day. A false "yes" is an unbroken run of "yes" forecasts that is not followed by an alert.
244	
245	The baseline and first model tables below use the threshold with the best F1, which was the working rule before the operating point was agreed (decision 21). The "Operating point" section gives the same models at the agreed thresholds.
246	
247	**Baselines**
248	
249	1. Climatology: frequency of an alert start by Kyiv hour × day of week.
250	2. Neighbour rule: "yes" if Kyiv oblast or an adjacent oblast (Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Cherkasy, Poltava, Vinnytsia — the five Ukrainian oblasts that border it, [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyiv_Oblast#Geography)) is under alert right now. Two variants are reported next to it: Kyiv oblast alone, and the number of these six regions under alert.
251	3. Logistic regression on the yes/no state of every region.
252	
253	For the "end" task: the empirical duration curve — P(end within `H` min | alert has lasted `t` min).
254	
255	**Time split** (no shuffling, gap ≥ `H` between parts)
256	
257	| Part | Period | Kyiv alert starts |
258	|---|---|---|
259	| Train | 2022-03-15 or 2024-07-01 (decision 14) … 2025-12-31 | 1,819 or 825 |
260	| Validation | 2026-01-01 … 2026-06-30 | 277 |
261	| Final training (train + validation) | … 2026-06-30 | 2,096 or 1,102 |
262	| Test | 2026-07-01 … 2026-09-06 | 171 |
263	
264	The split was changed after EDA. Options considered:
265	
266	| Option | Idea | Verdict |
267	|---|---|---|
268	| 1 | Keep validation at April–June 2026 | Every choice rests on 139 events; a rough error of ±8 percentage points on recall makes the comparison of training periods unreliable |
269	| 2 | Widen validation to January–June 2026 | 277 events and both winter and summer in validation, but training loses the 138 freshest alert starts and a third of the raion-level data |
270	| **3** | Option 2, then retrain the final model on train + validation | **chosen**: reliable choices and the freshest data in the final model |
271	| 4 | Rolling validation over several periods | Most reliable, too much code and time for a two-day MVP |
272	
273	Procedure: thresholds, hyperparameters, feature set and the training period are chosen on validation. They are then frozen, the model is retrained on train + validation with the same settings, and the test set is opened once.
274	
275	Cost of option 3: the threshold is picked for a model trained on less data and may be slightly off after retraining; this cannot be checked on anything but the test set.
276	
277	The test period is not moved even though it is unusually intense: choosing it to get a better number would be dishonest.
278	
279	### Baseline results
280	
281	Validation period, January–June 2026, 5-minute grid; produced by [scripts/baselines.py](scripts/baselines.py), full output in [reports/baselines_output.txt](reports/baselines_output.txt). The test period has not been touched. Thresholds are picked on the same validation data, so precision, recall and F1 are slightly optimistic, equally for every row.
282	
283	**"Start" task** — 49,187 points, 1,611 positive, base rate 3.28%.
284	
285	| Baseline | Trained on | PR-AUC | Precision | Recall | F1 | Says "yes" | False "yes" per day |
286	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
287	| Random | — | 3.2% | 3.3% | 91.9% | 6.4% | 91% of the time | 21.7 |
288	| Climatology | full history | 3.9% | 4.2% | 29.0% | 7.4% | 23% | 3.0 |
289	| Climatology | from 2024-07 | 3.9% | 4.7% | 28.2% | 8.0% | 20% | 1.5 |
290	| Rule: Kyiv oblast | — | 7.3% | 11.5% | 49.3% | 18.6% | 14% | 2.0 |
291	| Rule: Kyiv oblast or adjacent | — | 8.0% | 4.0% | 90.6% | 7.7% | 74% | 4.2 |
292	| Rule: at least 4 of the 6 neighbours | — | 8.0% | 13.4% | 22.1% | 16.7% | 5% | 1.2 |
293	| Logistic regression | full history | 9.7% | 14.7% | 33.0% | 20.3% | 7% | 2.0 |
294	| **Logistic regression** | **from 2024-07** | **11.3%** | 17.9% | 27.9% | **21.8%** | 5% | 1.5 |
295	
296	What this shows:
297	
298	- The bar is low: the best baseline has a PR-AUC of 11.3% and an F1 of 22%. The task is hard.
299	- Hour and day of week alone give almost nothing (3.9% against a 3.3% base rate). Forecasting from day and time only, an idea considered early on, would have produced exactly this.
300	- Adjacent oblasts matter as part of the picture, not as a switch. "Kyiv oblast or adjacent" catches 91% of alerts but says "yes" 74% of the time. Counting the neighbours instead of OR-ing them ranks better than Kyiv oblast alone (8.0% against 7.3%).
301	- Training from mid-2024 beats the full history for the logistic regression (11.3% against 9.7%), but only with the constant-feature filter of decision 16. Without it the recent variant scored 6.0%: the Kharkiv flag got a weight of −2.58 and the probability was inflated about 13 times whenever Kharkiv was not under alert (16% of the validation period).
302	
303	![Baselines, precision vs recall](reports/figures/baselines_start_pr.png)
304	![Baselines, calibration](reports/figures/baselines_start_calibration.png)
305	
306	**"End" task** — 2,936 points, base rate 46.3%.
307	
308	| Baseline | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | F1 |
309	|---|---|---|---|---|
310	| Always "yes" | — | 46.4% | — | 63.4% |
311	| Duration curve | full history | 60.6% | 0.2355 | 66.9% |
312	| Duration curve | from 2024-07 | 60.8% | 0.2309 | 67.0% |
313	
314	The duration curve ranks clearly better than chance but barely beats "always yes" on F1. With almost half of the points positive, F1 is a weak criterion for this task; PR-AUC and Brier are the ones to watch.
315	
316	For reference, the base rate of the "start" task grows with the horizon: 3.9% at 30 min, 7.4% at 60 min and 13.6% at 120 min (2026).
317	
318	### Model results
319	
320	First versions, validation period, same conditions as the baselines; produced by [scripts/models.py](scripts/models.py). LightGBM ran with the settings it had before tuning (15 leaves, minimum leaf 200). [saam/models.py](saam/models.py) now holds the tuned settings and [reports/models_output.txt](reports/models_output.txt) was regenerated with them, so that file matches the "after" numbers in "Tuning", not the tables of this section.
321	
322	**"Start" task** (base rate 3.28%)
323	
324	| Model | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | Precision | Recall | F1 | False "yes" per day |
325	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
326	| Best baseline (logistic regression) | full history | 9.7% | 0.0310 | 14.7% | 33.0% | 20.3% | 2.0 |
327	| Frequency table | full history | 10.0% | 0.0306 | 13.7% | 41.8% | 20.6% | 2.3 |
328	| **LightGBM** | full history | **12.8%** | 0.0302 | 20.9% | 29.4% | **24.4%** | 2.1 |
329	| Best baseline (logistic regression) | from 2024-07 | 11.3% | 0.0304 | 17.9% | 27.9% | 21.8% | 1.5 |
330	| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 9.9% | 0.0305 | 13.8% | 42.9% | 20.8% | 2.1 |
331	| LightGBM | from 2024-07 | 12.5% | 0.0302 | 19.6% | 30.8% | 23.9% | 2.4 |
332	
333	**"End" task** (base rate 46.3%)
334	
335	| Model | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | F1 |
336	|---|---|---|---|---|
337	| Baseline (duration curve) | full history | 60.6% | 0.2355 | 66.9% |
338	| Frequency table | full history | 63.4% | 0.2298 | 67.3% |
339	| LightGBM | full history | 72.2% | 0.2098 | 69.8% |
340	| Baseline (duration curve) | from 2024-07 | 60.8% | 0.2309 | 67.0% |
341	| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 64.5% | 0.2238 | 67.3% |
342	| **LightGBM** | from 2024-07 | **75.1%** | **0.1940** | **70.9%** |
343	
344	What this shows:
345	
346	- **"Start" is hard for every method.** LightGBM is the best, but its lead over the best baseline is modest: PR-AUC 12.5–12.8% against 11.3%, F1 24% against 22%.
347	- **The frequency table does not beat the best baseline on "start"** (10.0% against 11.3%): three factors are too few. It catches more alerts (recall 42–43%) at lower precision. On "end" it is ahead of the duration curve but far behind LightGBM.
348	- **"End" is where LightGBM clearly wins**: PR-AUC 75% against 61%.

375	### Operating point
376	
377	How the yes / no answer is cut out of the probability (decision 21). All numbers are from validation, LightGBM with the settings it had before tuning, mode "from 2024-07"; 277 Kyiv alerts in the period.

379	**"Start": the price of each recall level**
380	
381	| Recall by moments | Precision of "yes" | Says "yes" (share of quiet time) | False "yes" per day | Alerts warned |
382	|---|---|---|---|---|
383	| 30% | 19.5% | 5% | 2.3 | 47% |
384	| **40% (chosen)** | **15.0%** | **9%** | **3.6** | **55%** |
385	| 50% | 9.1% | 18% | 8.3 | 66% |
386	| 60% | 6.3% | 31% | 12.5 | 75% |
387	| 70% | 5.0% | 46% | 15.3 | 87% |
388	| 80% | 4.5% | 59% | 15.6 | 92% |

390	"Recall by moments" is the share of 5-minute moments before an alert at which the program said "yes". "Alerts warned" is the share of alerts preceded by at least one "yes" within 30 minutes — closer to what a user experiences, and always higher. For warned alerts the "yes" is typically already on at the start of the 30-minute window (median 25–27 min before the alert).
391	
392	The price rises steeply: beyond 60–70% the program says "yes" a third to a half of the time and turns into the "almost always yes" seen in the neighbour rule. At the chosen 40% it warns of a little over half of the alerts, says "yes" 9% of the quiet time, and about one "yes" in seven is right.

429	### Tuning
430	
431	A small search over LightGBM settings on validation ([scripts/tune.py](scripts/tune.py), output in [reports/tuning_output.txt](reports/tuning_output.txt) and [reports/tuning.csv](reports/tuning.csv)): 20 random combinations of the number of trees (150 / 300 / 600), learning rate (0.02 / 0.05 / 0.1), tree size (7 / 15 / 31 leaves) and minimum leaf size (100 / 300 / 1000), for each of the four models.
432	
433	**How much is noise.** The first settings were refitted with 5 random seeds. The seed alone moves the "start" PR-AUC by about ±0.5 percentage points (12.3–13.5% for full history, 11.8–13.3% for the recent period). This confirms that the earlier 12.5% against 12.8% between the two training periods was noise, and it sets the bar for any claimed improvement. With 20 candidates the best one is expected to look about two such deviations better by luck alone.
434	
435	**What was adopted.** Not the best candidate of each model, but one setting for all four: 7 leaves instead of 15 and a minimum leaf of 300 instead of 200 — smaller trees. It has the best average rank across the four models and is never the winner by a lucky margin in just one of them. Checked over 5 seeds each:
436	
437	| Model | PR-AUC before | PR-AUC after | At the operating point, before → after |
438	|---|---|---|---|
439	| "Start", full history | 12.9% ± 0.5 | 13.6% ± 0.4 | precision 15.4% → 15.4% |
440	| "Start", from 2024-07 | 12.6% ± 0.6 | 14.1% ± 0.4 | precision 14.9% → 15.5% |
441	| "End", full history | 72.6% ± 0.4 | 72.4% ± 0.3 | recall 82.0% → 85.2% |
442	| "End", from 2024-07 | 75.2% ± 0.2 | 76.0% ± 0.2 | recall 86.2% → 87.9% |
443	
444	The gain is clear for the default mode (from 2024-07): the new setting beats the best seed of the old one in 5 runs out of 5 in both tasks. For full history it is within noise. At the "start" operating point almost nothing changes: the ranking improved mostly in parts of the curve away from recall 40%. So tuning made the probabilities somewhat better and the yes / no answer barely different.
445	
446	What the search also showed: large trees with many boosting rounds are the worst (PR-AUC down to 8–10% on "start") — the model memorises the training period.

448	### Frozen before the test
449	
450	Everything that affects the test result was fixed, and committed, before the test period was opened. Nothing in this list is changed afterwards.
451	
452	1. Features: 112, region minutes capped at 180 (decisions 13, 18, 19).
453	2. Model: LightGBM with the settings from "Tuning". The final model is the average of 5 models that differ only in the random seed — this removes the ±0.5 points of seed noise found during tuning.
454	3. Modes: "from 2024-07" (default) and "full history" (decision 14).
455	4. Thresholds: recall ≥ 40% for "start", precision ≥ 60% for "end" (decision 21). Their values are computed on validation for models trained on the training period only, and are not adjusted on the test.
456	5. Final training on train + validation, up to 30 June 2026 (decision 15).
457	6. Test: 1 July – 6 September 2026, opened once. Both modes, the baselines and the frequency table are reported, each with a threshold picked on validation by the same rule.

504	### Uncertainty of the test results
505	
506	One test period of 68 days with 171 alerts; neighbouring 5-minute points are near-copies, so the effective sample is much smaller than the point counts suggest. To see how much of the differences could be chance, the test forecasts were resampled with a paired block bootstrap: [scripts/bootstrap.py](scripts/bootstrap.py), output in [reports/bootstrap_output.txt](reports/bootstrap_output.txt) and [reports/bootstrap.csv](reports/bootstrap.csv).
507	
508	Method: the period is cut into day-long blocks starting at 12:00 Kyiv time, so that a night attack stays in one block (69 blocks for "start", 54 with a Kyiv alert for "end"). Blocks are drawn with replacement 2,000 times, and both models of a comparison are scored on the same draw. The interval is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile. The rule was set before the run: if the interval of a difference contains zero, the two are reported as not distinguishable on this test.
509	
510	Nothing was tuned or re-chosen. LightGBM was loaded from `models/`. The two baselines had not been saved, so they were fitted again by the same deterministic procedure; the script checks that every reproduced metric equals the published one and stops otherwise.
511

513	|---|---|---|---|
514	| LightGBM, from 2024-07 | 18.9% | 13.0 … 26.7 | |
515	| Logistic regression, from 2024-07 | 17.1% | 11.2 … 24.5 | |
516	| LightGBM − logistic regression, from 2024-07 | +1.8 | −3.0 … +7.0 | not distinguishable |

534	What this says:
535	
536	- **"Start": both LightGBM and the logistic regression are clearly useful** (even the lower ends, 11–14%, are more than twice the 5.5% base rate), **but they cannot be ranked.** The same holds for the two training periods. The intervals are wide: the measured PR-AUC of 18.9% could plausibly have been anywhere from 13% to 27%.
537	- **"End": the miss is real, not bad luck.** The whole interval for LightGBM lies below the 60% target, and LightGBM's "yes" is less precise than the duration curve's. The two say "yes" at very different rates (88% against 49% of alert time), so this compares the two answers the program could give, not the models at equal recall.
538	
539	What the method does not show: the spread from retraining the models, and whether a future period will behave like this one. The days are also not fully independent — attack waves last several days — so the intervals are more likely too narrow than too wide.
540	
541	The validation period was used for many choices (feature cap, settings, thresholds), so validation numbers are optimistic; the gap between validation and test on "end" shows by how much they can be.

543	## Known limitations
544	
545	- **Data gap.** History ends on 2026-09-07; there is more than a month without data between training and live use.
546	- **Yellow and red alerts.** Since September 2026 alerts carry levels (yellow — drones, red — missiles); ubilling returns them. The model is trained on data without levels, so the live forecast is outside the training distribution and there is nothing to measure its quality on under the new regime. The introduction date (6 September) comes from a third-party project, not an official source.
547	- **Change of granularity.** Raion-level data barely exists before mid-2025, so raion-based features (decision 13) are degenerate in older years. For Chernihiv the oblast flag fires about twice as often after the move to raions.
548	- **Not all alerts are predictable from neighbours.** 37% of city alerts start with no alert in Kyiv oblast.
549	- **The "end" forecast is a weak hint.** On the test period its "yes" was right 45% of the time against a 60% target; the program says so under the answer.
550	- **The live source is volunteer-run.** Ubilling proxies third-party sources that do not always agree with each other; not for safety decisions.

| 2022 (from 15 Mar) | 1,010 | 505 | 541 |
| 2023 | 602 | 301 | 397 |
| 2024 | 1,004 | 502 | 542 |
| 2025 | 1,022 | 511 | 740 |
| 2026 (to 7 Sep) | 503 | 448 | 405 |
| **Total** | 4,141 | **2,267** | |

Duration: median 38 min, 95th percentile 231 min, maximum 673 min. No overlapping intervals. 10 alerts are shorter than 2 min; 29 pairs of alerts are less than 5 min apart (not merged, decision 5).

## Exploratory analysis

Done on a 1-minute grid (2.36M points, 2022-03-15 … 2026-09-07) with [scripts/eda.py](scripts/eda.py); the full numeric output is in [reports/eda_output.txt](reports/eda_output.txt). "Recent" below means from 2025-07-01. The analysis was run to answer six questions that the plan depended on.

### 1. Do neighbours predict Kyiv, and how early?

Yes. The strongest signal is Kyiv oblast: when it is under alert and the city is not, a city alert starts within 30 min in 12.5% of cases against a 3.5% base rate (recent).

- In 63% of city alert starts Kyiv oblast was already under alert; in 51% for at least 10 min, in 35% for at least 30 min; the median is 36 min.
- 37% of city alerts start with no alert in Kyiv oblast — these cannot be caught from neighbours.

The 30-minute horizon is kept: it matches the typical lead.

![Lead time](reports/figures/lead_time.png)

### 2. Which regions count as neighbours?

| Region | Share of time under alert | Precision | Lift | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kyiv oblast | 13% | 12.5% | 3.6× | 47% |
| Cherkasy | 8% | 11.0% | 3.1× | 26% |
| Zhytomyr | 5% | 8.7% | 2.5× | 13% |
| Poltava | 28% | 6.0% | 1.7× | 48% |
| Chernihiv | 60% | 4.7% | 1.3× | 81% |
| Sumy | 76% | 3.9% | 1.1× | 83% |
| Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk | 92–100% | ≈3.5% | 1.0× | 93–100% |

Recent period, Kyiv city quiet. Precision = P(city alert starts within 30 min | region under alert); recall = share of pre-alert minutes covered by the signal. Lift = precision divided by the 3.5% base rate.

Recall alone is misleading here: Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk reach 93–100% only because they are under alert almost all the time. Their lift of 1.0 means that knowing their state does not change the odds for Kyiv at all. They are kept as features anyway (decision 16).

Chernihiv, the motivating example of this project, gives 4.7% against a 3.5% base rate as a plain yes/no flag, because it is under alert most of the time. Western oblasts (Chernivtsi 12%, Vinnytsia 10%) are precise but rare: they switch on only during nationwide alerts, recall 2–6%. This is the reason for decision 13.

![Neighbour signal](reports/figures/neighbour_signal.png)

### 3. Did the move to raion-level alerts break the oblast flag?

Partly.

- Kyiv oblast: the share of time under alert jumped from 5.6% to 22.6% in the second half of 2024, while all its rows were still oblast-level. This is a real increase in attacks, not an aggregation effect. After the move to raions (2025) it stays at 17–26%.
- Chernihiv: here the effect is real — 28% → 55% → 68% right after the move.
- Kharkiv: 100% of the time from mid-2024 because of a single hromada-level alert that lasted 604 days.

![Share of time under alert](reports/figures/alert_share_heatmap.png)

### 4. Is it worth training on 2022–2023?

The data drifts:

- 2023 is the quietest year (301 alerts, 4.6% of the time under alert).
- Median duration falls: 49 → 55 → 34 → 35 → 30 min (2022 → 2026).
- Share of alerts starting at night (22:00–06:00 Kyiv time): 31% in 2022, 48% in 2025, 39% in 2026.
- After 2 hours of alert the chance to end within 30 min was 36% in 2022–2024 and 22% in 2025–2026.

Analysis alone cannot settle this, hence decision 14.

![Kyiv alerts per month](reports/figures/kyiv_alerts_per_month.png)
![Start hour by year](reports/figures/kyiv_start_hour_by_year.png)
![End curve](reports/figures/kyiv_end_curve.png)

### 5. How rare is the event?

- "Start" task: 3.0% of quiet minutes are followed by an alert within 30 min. This is the PR-AUC of random guessing.
- "End" task: 37% of alert minutes are followed by an end within 30 min.

With the split planned before EDA:

| Part | Kyiv alert starts | "Start" base rate |
|---|---|---|
| Train (to March 2026) | 1,957 | 2.9% |
| Validation (April–June 2026) | 139 | 3.3% |
| Test (July – 6 September 2026) | 171 | 5.5% |

The test period is about twice as intense as training: August 2026 had 90 alerts, the most since March 2022. Validation is small, so a threshold picked on 139 events would be noisy — this led to decision 15.

### 6. Data quality across all regions

- 2 rows with zero duration (Odesa and Kharkiv oblasts, November 2025) — dropped by the loader, 185,428 rows remain.
- 451 rows shorter than 1 min; 897 longer than 24 h, almost all in Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
- Overlapping intervals within the same raion or hromada: 0.
- Luhansk: 1 row; its permanent alert is not in the data, so the region is excluded.

## Time

The dataset is in UTC with a constant offset all year. Checked against known events: the mass strike of 2022-10-10 starts at 03:47 in the data, which is 06:47 Kyiv summer time.

The problem: Ukraine switches between UTC+2 (winter) and UTC+3 (summer), so the same UTC hour is a different hour for people. The data shows it: the peak of alert starts in Kyiv moves from 21:00 UTC in summer to 22:00–23:00 UTC in winter, while in Kyiv time it stays around midnight (2024–2026, small sample).

Options considered:

| Option | Idea | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Computations in UTC, calendar features in `Europe/Kyiv` | **chosen** |
| B | Convert the whole dataset to Kyiv time | The autumn hour 03:00–04:00 occurs twice, the spring one does not exist; an offset would have to be stored next to every timestamp |
| C | Everything in UTC + a "summer time" feature | Baselines cannot learn the shift, so the model comparison becomes unfair |
| D | Fixed offset all year | The hour is off by one for half of the year |

How A works: the time grid, region states, durations, lags and the target are computed in UTC, where a day is always 24 hours. For each grid point the Kyiv hour and day of week are computed separately with `zoneinfo`. On a switch night the grid stays regular; in autumn two neighbouring hours simply get the same label, and in spring one label is skipped.

No Kyiv alert in the dataset spans a switch moment (checked on all 9 switches); other oblasts were not checked.

## Evaluation

**Metrics**

- PR-AUC — primary (classes are imbalanced).
- Brier score and calibration curve.
- Precision / recall / F1 at a threshold picked on validation; the yes / no answer comes from this threshold.
- Number of false "yes" per day. A false "yes" is an unbroken run of "yes" forecasts that is not followed by an alert.

The baseline and first model tables below use the threshold with the best F1, which was the working rule before the operating point was agreed (decision 21). The "Operating point" section gives the same models at the agreed thresholds.

**Baselines**

1. Climatology: frequency of an alert start by Kyiv hour × day of week.
2. Neighbour rule: "yes" if Kyiv oblast or an adjacent oblast (Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Cherkasy, Poltava, Vinnytsia — the five Ukrainian oblasts that border it, [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyiv_Oblast#Geography)) is under alert right now. Two variants are reported next to it: Kyiv oblast alone, and the number of these six regions under alert.
3. Logistic regression on the yes/no state of every region.

For the "end" task: the empirical duration curve — P(end within `H` min | alert has lasted `t` min).

**Time split** (no shuffling, gap ≥ `H` between parts)

| Part | Period | Kyiv alert starts |
|---|---|---|
| Train | 2022-03-15 or 2024-07-01 (decision 14) … 2025-12-31 | 1,819 or 825 |
| Validation | 2026-01-01 … 2026-06-30 | 277 |
| Final training (train + validation) | … 2026-06-30 | 2,096 or 1,102 |
| Test | 2026-07-01 … 2026-09-06 | 171 |

The split was changed after EDA. Options considered:

| Option | Idea | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Keep validation at April–June 2026 | Every choice rests on 139 events; a rough error of ±8 percentage points on recall makes the comparison of training periods unreliable |
| 2 | Widen validation to January–June 2026 | 277 events and both winter and summer in validation, but training loses the 138 freshest alert starts and a third of the raion-level data |
| **3** | Option 2, then retrain the final model on train + validation | **chosen**: reliable choices and the freshest data in the final model |
| 4 | Rolling validation over several periods | Most reliable, too much code and time for a two-day MVP |

Procedure: thresholds, hyperparameters, feature set and the training period are chosen on validation. They are then frozen, the model is retrained on train + validation with the same settings, and the test set is opened once.

Cost of option 3: the threshold is picked for a model trained on less data and may be slightly off after retraining; this cannot be checked on anything but the test set.

The test period is not moved even though it is unusually intense: choosing it to get a better number would be dishonest.

### Baseline results

Validation period, January–June 2026, 5-minute grid; produced by [scripts/baselines.py](scripts/baselines.py), full output in [reports/baselines_output.txt](reports/baselines_output.txt). The test period has not been touched. Thresholds are picked on the same validation data, so precision, recall and F1 are slightly optimistic, equally for every row.

**"Start" task** — 49,187 points, 1,611 positive, base rate 3.28%.

| Baseline | Trained on | PR-AUC | Precision | Recall | F1 | Says "yes" | False "yes" per day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random | — | 3.2% | 3.3% | 91.9% | 6.4% | 91% of the time | 21.7 |
| Climatology | full history | 3.9% | 4.2% | 29.0% | 7.4% | 23% | 3.0 |
| Climatology | from 2024-07 | 3.9% | 4.7% | 28.2% | 8.0% | 20% | 1.5 |
| Rule: Kyiv oblast | — | 7.3% | 11.5% | 49.3% | 18.6% | 14% | 2.0 |
| Rule: Kyiv oblast or adjacent | — | 8.0% | 4.0% | 90.6% | 7.7% | 74% | 4.2 |
| Rule: at least 4 of the 6 neighbours | — | 8.0% | 13.4% | 22.1% | 16.7% | 5% | 1.2 |
| Logistic regression | full history | 9.7% | 14.7% | 33.0% | 20.3% | 7% | 2.0 |
| **Logistic regression** | **from 2024-07** | **11.3%** | 17.9% | 27.9% | **21.8%** | 5% | 1.5 |

What this shows:

- The bar is low: the best baseline has a PR-AUC of 11.3% and an F1 of 22%. The task is hard.
- Hour and day of week alone give almost nothing (3.9% against a 3.3% base rate). Forecasting from day and time only, an idea considered early on, would have produced exactly this.
- Adjacent oblasts matter as part of the picture, not as a switch. "Kyiv oblast or adjacent" catches 91% of alerts but says "yes" 74% of the time. Counting the neighbours instead of OR-ing them ranks better than Kyiv oblast alone (8.0% against 7.3%).
- Training from mid-2024 beats the full history for the logistic regression (11.3% against 9.7%), but only with the constant-feature filter of decision 16. Without it the recent variant scored 6.0%: the Kharkiv flag got a weight of −2.58 and the probability was inflated about 13 times whenever Kharkiv was not under alert (16% of the validation period).

![Baselines, precision vs recall](reports/figures/baselines_start_pr.png)
![Baselines, calibration](reports/figures/baselines_start_calibration.png)

**"End" task** — 2,936 points, base rate 46.3%.

| Baseline | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Always "yes" | — | 46.4% | — | 63.4% |
| Duration curve | full history | 60.6% | 0.2355 | 66.9% |
| Duration curve | from 2024-07 | 60.8% | 0.2309 | 67.0% |

The duration curve ranks clearly better than chance but barely beats "always yes" on F1. With almost half of the points positive, F1 is a weak criterion for this task; PR-AUC and Brier are the ones to watch.

For reference, the base rate of the "start" task grows with the horizon: 3.9% at 30 min, 7.4% at 60 min and 13.6% at 120 min (2026).

### Model results

First versions, validation period, same conditions as the baselines; produced by [scripts/models.py](scripts/models.py). LightGBM ran with the settings it had before tuning (15 leaves, minimum leaf 200). [saam/models.py](saam/models.py) now holds the tuned settings and [reports/models_output.txt](reports/models_output.txt) was regenerated with them, so that file matches the "after" numbers in "Tuning", not the tables of this section.

**"Start" task** (base rate 3.28%)

| Model | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | Precision | Recall | F1 | False "yes" per day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Best baseline (logistic regression) | full history | 9.7% | 0.0310 | 14.7% | 33.0% | 20.3% | 2.0 |
| Frequency table | full history | 10.0% | 0.0306 | 13.7% | 41.8% | 20.6% | 2.3 |
| **LightGBM** | full history | **12.8%** | 0.0302 | 20.9% | 29.4% | **24.4%** | 2.1 |
| Best baseline (logistic regression) | from 2024-07 | 11.3% | 0.0304 | 17.9% | 27.9% | 21.8% | 1.5 |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 9.9% | 0.0305 | 13.8% | 42.9% | 20.8% | 2.1 |
| LightGBM | from 2024-07 | 12.5% | 0.0302 | 19.6% | 30.8% | 23.9% | 2.4 |

**"End" task** (base rate 46.3%)

| Model | Trained on | PR-AUC | Brier | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (duration curve) | full history | 60.6% | 0.2355 | 66.9% |
| Frequency table | full history | 63.4% | 0.2298 | 67.3% |
| LightGBM | full history | 72.2% | 0.2098 | 69.8% |
| Baseline (duration curve) | from 2024-07 | 60.8% | 0.2309 | 67.0% |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 64.5% | 0.2238 | 67.3% |
| **LightGBM** | from 2024-07 | **75.1%** | **0.1940** | **70.9%** |

What this shows:

- **"Start" is hard for every method.** LightGBM is the best, but its lead over the best baseline is modest: PR-AUC 12.5–12.8% against 11.3%, F1 24% against 22%.
- **The frequency table does not beat the best baseline on "start"** (10.0% against 11.3%): three factors are too few. It catches more alerts (recall 42–43%) at lower precision. On "end" it is ahead of the duration curve but far behind LightGBM.
- **"End" is where LightGBM clearly wins**: PR-AUC 75% against 61%.
- **Training period (decision 14):** for "end" the recent period is better (75.1% against 72.2%); for "start" the two are within noise of each other (12.5% against 12.8%). Both are kept as modes of the program.

What the models look at (LightGBM, share of total gain):

- "Start": Kyiv oblast and its raions give 29–38%, the calendar about 11%, all other regions together about half.
- "End": the top features are how recently a new alert started in Chernihiv and Poltava oblasts. The duration of the Kyiv alert itself gives only 2–4%: the model judges the end by whether the attack is still unfolding at the neighbours.

The most and least likely cells of the "start" frequency table (trained from 2024-07; full tables in [reports/frequency_table_start.csv](reports/frequency_table_start.csv) and [reports/frequency_table_end.csv](reports/frequency_table_end.csv)):

| Kyiv oblast | Adjacent oblasts under alert | Time of day | Training points | Chance of a Kyiv alert within 30 min |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| alert 15–60 min | 3+ | night | 1,823 | 23.3% |
| alert 15–60 min | 3+ | evening | 425 | 19.9% |
| alert < 15 min | 3+ | night | 595 | 18.7% |
| quiet | 0 | morning | 24,122 | 1.3% |
| quiet | 0 | night | 15,945 | 1.1% |

**The hidden clock (decision 19).** On the first run LightGBM lost to the logistic regression on the recent period (10.4% against 11.3%). Its third most important feature was "minutes since the oldest active alert in Kharkiv oblast started" — a counter of days since May 2024. Three variants were compared on validation: as is, minutes capped at 180, and capped with the "oldest" features removed. The cap value was taken from EDA (neighbours lead Kyiv by tens of minutes), not searched for.

| "Start" task, LightGBM | Full history: PR-AUC / Brier | From 2024-07: PR-AUC / Brier |
|---|---|---|
| Uncapped | 11.3% / 0.0319 | 10.4% / 0.0366 |
| Capped at 180 min | 12.8% / 0.0302 | 12.5% / 0.0302 |

Removing the "oldest" features on top of the cap gave nothing and was not adopted.

### Operating point

How the yes / no answer is cut out of the probability (decision 21). All numbers are from validation, LightGBM with the settings it had before tuning, mode "from 2024-07"; 277 Kyiv alerts in the period.

**"Start": the price of each recall level**

| Recall by moments | Precision of "yes" | Says "yes" (share of quiet time) | False "yes" per day | Alerts warned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30% | 19.5% | 5% | 2.3 | 47% |
| **40% (chosen)** | **15.0%** | **9%** | **3.6** | **55%** |
| 50% | 9.1% | 18% | 8.3 | 66% |
| 60% | 6.3% | 31% | 12.5 | 75% |
| 70% | 5.0% | 46% | 15.3 | 87% |
| 80% | 4.5% | 59% | 15.6 | 92% |

"Recall by moments" is the share of 5-minute moments before an alert at which the program said "yes". "Alerts warned" is the share of alerts preceded by at least one "yes" within 30 minutes — closer to what a user experiences, and always higher. For warned alerts the "yes" is typically already on at the start of the 30-minute window (median 25–27 min before the alert).

The price rises steeply: beyond 60–70% the program says "yes" a third to a half of the time and turns into the "almost always yes" seen in the neighbour rule. At the chosen 40% it warns of a little over half of the alerts, says "yes" 9% of the quiet time, and about one "yes" in seven is right.

**"End": the price of each precision level**

| Precision of "yes, it will end" | Real endings caught | Says "yes" (share of alert time) |
|---|---|---|
| **60% (chosen)** | **86%** | **67%** |
| 70% | 64% | 42% |
| 80% | 43% | 25% |
| 90% | 20% | 10% |

At the chosen 60%, four in ten promises of an all-clear within 30 minutes are wrong. The base rate is 46%, so the gain over saying "yes" always is 14 points of precision.

**All models at the agreed operating point**

| "Start", recall ≥ 40% | Trained on | Precision | Says "yes" | False "yes" per day | Alerts warned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Best baseline (logistic regression) | full history | 12.2% | 10.7% | 2.8 | 54% |
| Frequency table | full history | 13.7% | 9.6% | 2.3 | 53% |
| LightGBM | full history | 16.0% | 8.2% | 3.2 | 57% |
| Best baseline (logistic regression) | from 2024-07 | 13.4% | 9.9% | 2.2 | 53% |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 13.6% | 9.7% | 2.2 | 53% |
| LightGBM | from 2024-07 | 15.0% | 8.8% | 3.6 | 55% |

| "End", precision ≥ 60% | Trained on | Real endings caught | Says "yes" |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (duration curve) | full history | 71% | 54% |
| Frequency table | full history | 68% | 51% |
| LightGBM | full history | 81% | 63% |
| Baseline (duration curve) | from 2024-07 | 71% | 54% |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 66% | 49% |
| LightGBM | from 2024-07 | 86% | 67% |

LightGBM is the most precise at the same recall and says "yes" for the least time, but its "yes" comes in more separate episodes, so it has more false episodes per day than the simpler methods (3.2–3.6 against 2.2–2.8).

The thresholds are picked on validation. The test period is more intense, so the actual recall and precision there may differ from 40% and 60%.

### Tuning

A small search over LightGBM settings on validation ([scripts/tune.py](scripts/tune.py), output in [reports/tuning_output.txt](reports/tuning_output.txt) and [reports/tuning.csv](reports/tuning.csv)): 20 random combinations of the number of trees (150 / 300 / 600), learning rate (0.02 / 0.05 / 0.1), tree size (7 / 15 / 31 leaves) and minimum leaf size (100 / 300 / 1000), for each of the four models.

**How much is noise.** The first settings were refitted with 5 random seeds. The seed alone moves the "start" PR-AUC by about ±0.5 percentage points (12.3–13.5% for full history, 11.8–13.3% for the recent period). This confirms that the earlier 12.5% against 12.8% between the two training periods was noise, and it sets the bar for any claimed improvement. With 20 candidates the best one is expected to look about two such deviations better by luck alone.

**What was adopted.** Not the best candidate of each model, but one setting for all four: 7 leaves instead of 15 and a minimum leaf of 300 instead of 200 — smaller trees. It has the best average rank across the four models and is never the winner by a lucky margin in just one of them. Checked over 5 seeds each:

| Model | PR-AUC before | PR-AUC after | At the operating point, before → after |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Start", full history | 12.9% ± 0.5 | 13.6% ± 0.4 | precision 15.4% → 15.4% |
| "Start", from 2024-07 | 12.6% ± 0.6 | 14.1% ± 0.4 | precision 14.9% → 15.5% |
| "End", full history | 72.6% ± 0.4 | 72.4% ± 0.3 | recall 82.0% → 85.2% |
| "End", from 2024-07 | 75.2% ± 0.2 | 76.0% ± 0.2 | recall 86.2% → 87.9% |

The gain is clear for the default mode (from 2024-07): the new setting beats the best seed of the old one in 5 runs out of 5 in both tasks. For full history it is within noise. At the "start" operating point almost nothing changes: the ranking improved mostly in parts of the curve away from recall 40%. So tuning made the probabilities somewhat better and the yes / no answer barely different.

What the search also showed: large trees with many boosting rounds are the worst (PR-AUC down to 8–10% on "start") — the model memorises the training period.

### Frozen before the test

Everything that affects the test result was fixed, and committed, before the test period was opened. Nothing in this list is changed afterwards.

1. Features: 112, region minutes capped at 180 (decisions 13, 18, 19).
2. Model: LightGBM with the settings from "Tuning". The final model is the average of 5 models that differ only in the random seed — this removes the ±0.5 points of seed noise found during tuning.
3. Modes: "from 2024-07" (default) and "full history" (decision 14).
4. Thresholds: recall ≥ 40% for "start", precision ≥ 60% for "end" (decision 21). Their values are computed on validation for models trained on the training period only, and are not adjusted on the test.
5. Final training on train + validation, up to 30 June 2026 (decision 15).
6. Test: 1 July – 6 September 2026, opened once. Both modes, the baselines and the frequency table are reported, each with a threshold picked on validation by the same rule.

### Test results

One pass over 1 July – 6 September 2026 with the frozen protocol; produced by [scripts/final.py](scripts/final.py), full output in [reports/final_output.txt](reports/final_output.txt). 171 Kyiv alerts in the period. Nothing was changed after seeing these numbers.

**"Start": will a Kyiv alert start within 30 minutes** — 17,664 points, base rate 5.47% (validation: 3.28%)

| Model | Mode | PR-AUC | Precision | Recall | Says "yes" | False "yes" per day | Alerts warned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline: climatology | from 2024-07 | 7.4% | 6.8% | 42.1% | 33.7% | 2.2 | 44% |
| Baseline: logistic regression | from 2024-07 | 17.1% | 13.8% | 39.3% | 15.6% | 2.3 | 61% |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 15.7% | 23.6% | 34.5% | 8.0% | 2.2 | 56% |
| **LightGBM (default mode)** | from 2024-07 | 18.9% | 17.9% | 38.4% | 11.7% | 2.4 | **64%** |
| Baseline: logistic regression | full history | 19.4% | 14.5% | 43.2% | 16.3% | 2.3 | 63% |
| Frequency table | full history | 15.8% | 23.7% | 35.6% | 8.2% | 2.2 | 57% |
| LightGBM | full history | **19.8%** | 26.6% | 35.7% | 7.3% | 2.6 | 63% |

Reference: saying "yes" always gives 5.5% precision.

- **The forecast held up.** In the default mode the program warned of 64% of the alerts, said "yes" 11.7% of the quiet time, and about one "yes" in six was right — more than three times the base rate. Recall came out at 38.4% against the 40% target: the threshold transferred well.
- **LightGBM is the best by PR-AUC, but not by much.** Its lead over the logistic regression is 1.8 points in the default mode and 0.4 points on full history. The bootstrap below shows that a difference of this size is well within chance, so LightGBM cannot be claimed to be better than the regression on new data. Its advantage on validation (14.3% against 11.3%) shrank on the test.
- **The default mode was not the better one on the test** (18.9% against 19.8%). It was named before the test and stays the default; the difference is within the seed noise measured earlier.
- **The frequency table does better than expected at its threshold**: the highest precision among the simple methods (23.6%) at a somewhat lower recall.
- The probabilities are too low on average (3.6% predicted against 5.5% observed): the test period is more intense than anything the models were trained on.

![Test, precision vs recall](reports/figures/test_start_pr.png)
![Forecast vs actual alerts](reports/figures/test_timeline.png)

**"End": will the current alert end within 30 minutes** — 1,915 points, base rate 41.1% (validation: 46.3%)

| Model | Mode | PR-AUC | Brier | Precision of "yes" | Real endings caught | Says "yes" |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline: duration curve | from 2024-07 | 50.9% | 0.233 | 52.0% | 62% | 49% |
| Frequency table | from 2024-07 | 50.7% | 0.239 | 47.4% | 72% | 62% |
| **LightGBM (default mode)** | from 2024-07 | 55.9% | 0.252 | **45.2%** | 97% | 88% |
| Baseline: duration curve | full history | 51.4% | 0.230 | 52.0% | 62% | 49% |
| Frequency table | full history | 49.1% | 0.234 | 46.2% | 68% | 60% |
| LightGBM | full history | 58.8% | 0.228 | 44.8% | 96% | 88% |

- **The target was not met.** The agreed rule was that a "yes, it will end" is right at least 60% of the time. On the test it was right 45% of the time, and the program said "yes" during 88% of alert time. At this threshold the forecast is barely better than always saying "yes" (41%), and no method reached 60%.
- **The model's quality dropped, not only the threshold.** PR-AUC fell from 76% on validation to 56% on the test. In the default mode the Brier score (0.252) is worse than that of the simple duration curve (0.233) and worse than predicting the base rate for every point (0.242). LightGBM still ranks moments better than the baselines (PR-AUC 56–59% against 51%), but its probabilities are too high: 55% predicted on average against 41% observed.
- **Diagnostics after the fact** (they explain the result and change nothing): the model that was not retrained on validation gives the same 46% precision, so the final retraining is not the cause. Even with hindsight, 60% precision is reachable on the test only for 20–40% of the endings. Alert durations in the test period look like those in validation (median 30 min against 29), so the change is in how the neighbours' state relates to the end of a Kyiv alert.
- **What follows for the program (decision 22):** the "end" answer stays a yes / no, as agreed at the start. Claude proposed showing only the probability; the author kept the binary answer. The measured precision of 45% is stated here and printed under the answer every time the "end" question is shown, so the weakness is in front of the user rather than hidden.

![Test, calibration](reports/figures/test_calibration.png)

### Uncertainty of the test results

One test period of 68 days with 171 alerts; neighbouring 5-minute points are near-copies, so the effective sample is much smaller than the point counts suggest. To see how much of the differences could be chance, the test forecasts were resampled with a paired block bootstrap: [scripts/bootstrap.py](scripts/bootstrap.py), output in [reports/bootstrap_output.txt](reports/bootstrap_output.txt) and [reports/bootstrap.csv](reports/bootstrap.csv).

Method: the period is cut into day-long blocks starting at 12:00 Kyiv time, so that a night attack stays in one block (69 blocks for "start", 54 with a Kyiv alert for "end"). Blocks are drawn with replacement 2,000 times, and both models of a comparison are scored on the same draw. The interval is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile. The rule was set before the run: if the interval of a difference contains zero, the two are reported as not distinguishable on this test.

Nothing was tuned or re-chosen. LightGBM was loaded from `models/`. The two baselines had not been saved, so they were fitted again by the same deterministic procedure; the script checks that every reproduced metric equals the published one and stops otherwise.

| "Start", PR-AUC | Value | 95% interval | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| LightGBM, from 2024-07 | 18.9% | 13.0 … 26.7 | |
| Logistic regression, from 2024-07 | 17.1% | 11.2 … 24.5 | |
| LightGBM − logistic regression, from 2024-07 | +1.8 | −3.0 … +7.0 | not distinguishable |
| LightGBM, full history | 19.8% | 13.7 … 27.6 | |
| Logistic regression, full history | 19.4% | 12.3 … 28.2 | |
| LightGBM − logistic regression, full history | +0.4 | −5.5 … +5.9 | not distinguishable |
| LightGBM: from 2024-07 − full history | −0.9 | −2.4 … +1.2 | not distinguishable |
| Logistic regression: from 2024-07 − full history | −2.3 | −5.2 … +0.5 | not distinguishable |

| "End", precision of "yes" at the frozen thresholds | Value | 95% interval | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| LightGBM, from 2024-07 | 45.2% | 38.4 … 53.5 | the 60% target is outside the interval |
| Duration curve, from 2024-07 | 52.0% | 44.0 … 60.0 | |
| LightGBM − duration curve, from 2024-07 | −6.8 | −12.3 … −1.6 | LightGBM is worse |
| LightGBM, full history | 44.8% | 38.0 … 53.1 | the 60% target is outside the interval |
| LightGBM − duration curve, full history | −7.2 | −12.5 … −2.0 | LightGBM is worse |
| LightGBM: from 2024-07 − full history | +0.4 | −0.0 … +0.9 | not distinguishable |
| Always "yes" (base rate) | 41.1% | 33.7 … 50.2 | |
| LightGBM, from 2024-07 − always "yes" | +4.1 | +0.3 … +9.6 | slightly better than always "yes" |

What this says:

- **"Start": both LightGBM and the logistic regression are clearly useful** (even the lower ends, 11–14%, are more than twice the 5.5% base rate), **but they cannot be ranked.** The same holds for the two training periods. The intervals are wide: the measured PR-AUC of 18.9% could plausibly have been anywhere from 13% to 27%.
- **"End": the miss is real, not bad luck.** The whole interval for LightGBM lies below the 60% target, and LightGBM's "yes" is less precise than the duration curve's. The two say "yes" at very different rates (88% against 49% of alert time), so this compares the two answers the program could give, not the models at equal recall.

What the method does not show: the spread from retraining the models, and whether a future period will behave like this one. The days are also not fully independent — attack waves last several days — so the intervals are more likely too narrow than too wide.

The validation period was used for many choices (feature cap, settings, thresholds), so validation numbers are optimistic; the gap between validation and test on "end" shows by how much they can be.

## Known limitations

- **Data gap.** History ends on 2026-09-07; there is more than a month without data between training and live use.
- **Yellow and red alerts.** Since September 2026 alerts carry levels (yellow — drones, red — missiles); ubilling returns them. The model is trained on data without levels, so the live forecast is outside the training distribution and there is nothing to measure its quality on under the new regime. The introduction date (6 September) comes from a third-party project, not an official source.
- **Change of granularity.** Raion-level data barely exists before mid-2025, so raion-based features (decision 13) are degenerate in older years. For Chernihiv the oblast flag fires about twice as often after the move to raions.
- **Not all alerts are predictable from neighbours.** 37% of city alerts start with no alert in Kyiv oblast.
- **The "end" forecast is a weak hint.** On the test period its "yes" was right 45% of the time against a 60% target; the program says so under the answer.
- **The live source is volunteer-run.** Ubilling proxies third-party sources that do not always agree with each other; not for safety decisions.

import sys

p = sys.argv[1]
s = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()


def rep(a, b):
    global s
    assert s.count(a) == 1, (a[:70], s.count(a))
    s = s.replace(a, b)


def whole_line(start, new):
    global s
    assert s.count(start) == 1, (start, s.count(start))
    i = s.index(start)
    j = s.index("\n", i)
    s = s[:i] + new + s[j:]


def after_line(start, text):
    global s
    assert s.count(start) == 1, (start, s.count(start))
    i = s.index(start)
    j = s.index("\n", i)
    s = s[:j] + "\n" + text + s[j:]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- top

    "Default `H` = 30 min. The user-facing output is binary (yes / no); probabilities and technical details live in the `--debug` panel and in the figures of this README.")
after_line("- noticed that the 93–100% recall of frontline regions meant only \"always under alert\", not a signal.",

           "| 7 | Time: storage and all interval computations in **UTC**; hour of day and day of week in **Kyiv time** (`Europe/Kyiv`). "

whole_line("| 18 | Features use only a snapshot",

"""Features and targets on a time grid.

Every feature at time t is computed only from a snapshot of the state at t:
which alerts are active and when they started. Nothing about alerts that
have already ended is used: the live API does not report it, and the models
were trained and tested without it (README, decisions 18 and 23). An alert's
end time is used only as "has it ended by t". The same code serves history
and live data.

All arithmetic is in UTC epoch seconds; Kyiv-local calendar values are
derived separately (README, "Time", option A).
"""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from .config import MINUTES_CAP
from .data import KYIV_CITY, KYIV_TZ, REGION_EN

EXCLUDED = {"Луганська область"}  # permanent alert, absent from the data
FEATURE_REGIONS = [r for r in REGION_EN if r not in EXCLUDED and r != KYIV_CITY]
KYIV_OBLAST = "Київська область"

# Raions per oblast. Fixed so that history and live data use the same
# denominator; equal to the counts in the dataset and in the ubilling API.
RAION_COUNT = {
    "Вінницька область": 6, "Волинська область": 4, "Дніпропетровська область": 7,
    "Донецька область": 8, "Житомирська область": 4, "Закарпатська область": 6,
    "Запорізька область": 5, "Івано-Франківська область": 6, "Київська область": 7,
    "Кіровоградська область": 4, "Львівська область": 7, "Миколаївська область": 4,
    "Одеська область": 7, "Полтавська область": 4, "Рівненська область": 4,
    "Сумська область": 5, "Тернопільська область": 3, "Харківська область": 7,
    "Херсонська область": 5, "Хмельницька область": 3, "Черкаська область": 4,
    "Чернівецька область": 3, "Чернігівська область": 5,
}
KYIV_OBLAST_RAIONS = {
    "Бориспільський район": "boryspil", "Броварський район": "brovary",
    "Бучанський район": "bucha", "Білоцерківський район": "bila_tserkva",
    "Вишгородський район": "vyshhorod", "Обухівський район": "obukhiv",
    "Фастівський район": "fastiv",
}


def _slug(region):
    return REGION_EN[region].lower().replace(" ", "_").replace("-", "_")


def _epoch(series):
    return series.to_numpy("datetime64[s]").astype("int64")


def make_grid(start, end, step_min):
    """Regular UTC grid of epoch seconds in [start, end)."""
    s = int(pd.Timestamp(start, tz="UTC").timestamp())
    e = int(pd.Timestamp(end, tz="UTC").timestamp())
    return np.arange(s, e, step_min * 60, dtype="int64")


def _elapsed(starts, ends, grid):
    """Minutes since the start of the alert active at each grid instant, NaN
    where none is active. `starts`/`ends` must be sorted and non-overlapping."""
    if len(starts) == 0:
        return np.full(len(grid), np.nan)
    k = np.searchsorted(starts, grid, "right") - 1
    kc = np.clip(k, 0, None)
    active = (k >= 0) & (ends[kc] > grid)
    return np.where(active, (grid - starts[kc]) / 60.0, np.nan)


def _cap(minutes):
    """Cap "minutes since an alert started" at MINUTES_CAP, i.e. "long ago".
    Uncapped, the value for a region with a months-long alert is a day
    counter and lets a model learn the calendar date."""
    return np.minimum(minutes, MINUTES_CAP).astype("float32")


def _region_block(g, grid):
    """Per-raion elapsed minutes for one oblast.

    Returns (by_raion, oblast_level): `by_raion` maps a raion name to the
    elapsed-minutes arrays of every alert series inside it (the raion itself
    and its hromadas); `oblast_level` is the list for oblast-wide alerts.
    """
    by_raion, oblast_level = {}, []
    for (raion, _), u in g.groupby(["raion", "hromada"], sort=False):
        s, e = _epoch(u["started_at"]), _epoch(u["finished_at"])
        order = np.argsort(s, kind="stable")
        el = _elapsed(s[order], e[order], grid)
        (by_raion.setdefault(raion, []) if raion else oblast_level).append(el)
    return by_raion, oblast_level


def _nan_reduce(arrays, fn, n):
    if not arrays:
        return np.full(n, np.nan)
    stacked = np.vstack(arrays)
    out = np.full(n, np.nan)
    has = ~np.isnan(stacked).all(axis=0)
    out[has] = fn(stacked[:, has], axis=0)
    return out


def build_features(df, grid):
    """Feature table for the given grid (epoch seconds, UTC).

    `df` holds alert rows: oblast, raion, hromada, started_at, finished_at.
    """
    n = len(grid)
    cols = {}
    regions_on = np.zeros(n)
    groups = dict(tuple(df.groupby("oblast", sort=False)))

    for region in FEATURE_REGIONS:
        name = _slug(region)
        g = groups.get(region)
        by_raion, oblast_level = _region_block(g, grid) if g is not None else ({}, [])
        whole = _nan_reduce(oblast_level, np.nanmin, n)  # oblast-wide alert active
        raion_el = {r: _nan_reduce(a, np.nanmin, n) for r, a in by_raion.items()}

        everything = oblast_level + [a for arrs in by_raion.values() for a in arrs]
        newest = _nan_reduce(everything, np.nanmin, n)
        oldest = _nan_reduce(everything, np.nanmax, n)
        on = ~np.isnan(newest)

        n_raions_on = sum((~np.isnan(a)).astype(float) for a in raion_el.values()) if raion_el else np.zeros(n)
        share = np.where(~np.isnan(whole), 1.0, n_raions_on / RAION_COUNT[region])

        cols[f"{name}_on"] = on.astype("float32")
        cols[f"{name}_share"] = share.astype("float32")
        cols[f"{name}_newest_min"] = _cap(newest)
        cols[f"{name}_oldest_min"] = _cap(oldest)
        regions_on += on

        if region == KYIV_OBLAST:
            for raion, short in KYIV_OBLAST_RAIONS.items():
                # an oblast-wide alert covers every raion
                parts = [a for a in (raion_el.get(raion), whole) if a is not None]
                el = _nan_reduce(parts, np.nanmin, n)
                cols[f"ko_{short}_on"] = (~np.isnan(el)).astype("float32")
                cols[f"ko_{short}_min"] = _cap(el)

    cols["regions_on"] = regions_on.astype("float32")

    ky_s, ky_e = kyiv_intervals(df)
    cols["kyiv_on_min"] = _elapsed(ky_s, ky_e, grid).astype("float32")

    local = pd.to_datetime(grid, unit="s", utc=True).tz_convert(KYIV_TZ)
    hour = local.hour + local.minute / 60.0
    cols["hour_kyiv"] = local.hour.to_numpy("float32")
    cols["dow_kyiv"] = local.dayofweek.to_numpy("float32")
    cols["hour_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * hour / 24).astype("float32")
    cols["hour_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * hour / 24).astype("float32")

    return pd.DataFrame(cols, index=pd.to_datetime(grid, unit="s", utc=True))


def kyiv_intervals(df):
    """Sorted (starts, ends) of Kyiv city alerts, epoch seconds."""
    k = df[df["oblast"] == KYIV_CITY]
    s, e = _epoch(k["started_at"]), _epoch(k["finished_at"])
    order = np.argsort(s, kind="stable")
    return s[order], e[order]


def build_targets(df, grid, horizon_min):
    """Targets for both tasks.

    y_start: a Kyiv alert starts in (t, t+H]; meaningful where `quiet`.
    y_end:   the active Kyiv alert ends in (t, t+H]; meaningful where not `quiet`.
    """
    h = horizon_min * 60
    ky_s, ky_e = kyiv_intervals(df)
    nxt = np.searchsorted(ky_s, grid, "right")
    has_next = nxt < len(ky_s)
    y_start = np.zeros(len(grid), bool)
    y_start[has_next] = ky_s[nxt[has_next]] - grid[has_next] <= h

    cur = nxt - 1
    cc = np.clip(cur, 0, None)
    active = (cur >= 0) & (ky_e[cc] > grid)
    y_end = active & (ky_e[cc] - grid <= h)

    idx = pd.to_datetime(grid, unit="s", utc=True)
    return pd.DataFrame({"quiet": ~active, "y_start": y_start & ~active, "y_end": y_end}, index=idx)

Перечитав README повністю (усі 619 рядків) і звірив із кодом. Знайшов і виправив одну справжню суперечність навколо «моніторингу», два пропущені твої рішення, кілька застарілих тверджень і одне речення з помилками. Коміт `32d0c46` локальний, не запушений; 31 тест проходить.

## Моніторинг: що було не так

Суперечність створив я. Коли ти попросив, щоб програма оновлювалась сама, я записав, що це «скасовує припущення рішення 18», і назвав це суперечністю. Причина ж у тебе була інша — тривалість сесії, а не слово «монітор».

Тепер скрізь одна версія:
- **Рішення 18:** ознаку «хвилин від останнього відбою» прибрано, бо ніхто не триматиме програму відкритою довше приблизно пів години, тож вона рідко бачила б потрібний відбій, а стеження за станом заради однієї помірної ознаки — марна трата зусиль. Записано, що це твоє рішення, не моє.
- **Рішення 23:** оновлення екрана потрібне, щоб не перезапускати програму протягом сесії. Воно не робить програму монітором і рішенню 18 не суперечить.
- **Розширення в кінці:** пункт «тепер можна додати цю ознаку» замінено на «не планується».
- **Докстрінг у `saam/features.py`** приведено до тієї ж причини.

## Як ти мене зупинив — винесено

- **«In short»:** четвертий пункт серед твоїх правок — ти зупинив мене, коли я запропонував рішення, що мовчки припускало довготривалий монітор.
- **Рішення 18 і рядок журналу:** прямо сказано, що я сам, не питаючи, вирішив, ніби програма — монітор, і що ти зупинив це до написання коду.
- **Новий рядок журналу:** моя хибна «суперечність» між рішеннями 18 і 23 і твоє виправлення.

Через четвертий пункт «In short» тепер має 11 рядків замість 10. Якщо ліміт важливий — скажи, який пункт прибрати.

## Пропущені рішення, які ти приймав

1. **Лише київська година.** Я пропонував дати моделі ще й московську (там немає переходу на літній час) і порівняти; ти обрав одну київську. Додано в рішення 7, у розділ «Time» і в журнал. Московську годину так і не пробували — це теж сказано.
2. **Моделі в репозиторії.** Твоє «коміть разом з моделями» ніде не було записане як рішення. Тепер це рішення 24.

Решту твоїх рішень я звірив із розмовою — вони в таблиці або в журналі.

## Граматика

Єдине місце з помилками — речення, яке ти дописав у рішення 23 («overengeeniring», «decsision», «That's was»). Його зміст збережено й перенесено в рішення 18: «This was the author's decision, not Claude's». Інших помилок у тексті я не знайшов.

## Інші розбіжності

- **«Nothing was changed after seeing these numbers»** у результатах тесту — неточно, бо пізніше змінювався показ і додавався бутстреп. Тепер: не змінювались моделі, ознаки й пороги.
- **Рішення 16** обіцяло, що порівняння «покаже» вплив прихованого годинника, у майбутньому часі. Замінено на результат: режими на тесті не відрізняються.
- **«End is where LightGBM clearly wins»** у розділі про валідацію читалось як підсумок. Додано, що це на валідації й що тест цього не підтвердив.
- **Режим за замовчуванням на тесті:** пояснення «в межах шуму зерен» замінено на число з бутстрепу (−0,9, інтервал −2,4 … +1,2).
- **69 блоків при 68 днях** — додано, звідки зайвий блок.
- **Перший абзац** казав, що деталі «в дашбордах»; тепер — у панелі `--debug` і в графіках README.
- **«Why Kyiv only»** називало Чернігівську прикладом сильного сусіда; додано посилання на EDA, де вона виявилась слабким сигналом сама по собі.

## Чого я не чіпав

- Журнал правок залишив повним, включно з рядком про «not left running» — там це цитата того, що було виправлено.
- Рядок «Author → author», який ти видалив раніше, не повертав.

```bash
git push
```

"""Why the "end" yes / no answer is worse than the baseline on the test period.

Run from the repository root:  python -X utf8 scripts/end_diagnostics.py

Diagnostics only: nothing is tuned, chosen or changed. LightGBM is loaded from
models/ and is not retrained. The duration curve was not saved, so it is
fitted again by the same deterministic procedure as in scripts/final.py and
checked against the published numbers. Validation figures are quoted from
reports/final_output.txt, because the validation-stage LightGBM was not saved.
"""
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import joblib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from saam import config as C
from saam.baselines import DurationCurve
from saam.data import KYIV_TZ
from saam.dataset import load_dataset, period_mask
from saam.metrics import threshold_for_precision

MODE, FNAME, TSTART = "from 2024-07", "from_2024_07", C.TRAIN_START_RECENT  # the default mode
# reports/final_output.txt, END / VALIDATION, mode "from 2024-07": precision, recall, says yes (percent)
VAL = {"LightGBM": (60.0, 88.2, 68.1), "duration curve": (60.7, 70.7, 54.0)}
VAL_PR_AUC = {"LightGBM": 76.2, "duration curve": 60.8}

X, Y = load_dataset()
quiet = Y["quiet"].to_numpy()
alert = ~quiet
train = period_mask(X.index, TSTART, C.TRAIN_END) & alert
val = period_mask(X.index, C.VAL_START, C.VAL_END) & alert
final = period_mask(X.index, TSTART, C.VAL_END) & alert
test = period_mask(X.index, C.TEST_START, C.TEST_END) & alert
y = Y["y_end"][test].to_numpy()

thr_lgbm = json.loads((ROOT / "models" / "thresholds.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))[f"end/{MODE}"]
p_lgbm = joblib.load(ROOT / "models" / f"lgbm_end_{FNAME}.joblib").predict_proba(X[test])
thr_curve = threshold_for_precision(Y["y_end"][val].to_numpy(), DurationCurve().fit(X[train], Y["y_end"][train].to_numpy()).predict_proba(X[val]), C.END_MIN_PRECISION)
p_curve = DurationCurve().fit(X[final], Y["y_end"][final].to_numpy()).predict_proba(X[test])


def stats(pred):
    return 100 * (pred & y).sum() / max(pred.sum(), 1), 100 * (pred & y).sum() / y.sum(), 100 * pred.mean()


got = {"LightGBM": stats(p_lgbm >= thr_lgbm), "duration curve": stats(p_curve >= thr_curve)}
if round(got["LightGBM"][0], 1) != 45.2 or round(got["duration curve"][0], 1) != 52.0:
    sys.exit(f"STOP: reproduced precision {got} differs from the published 45.2% / 52.0%")
print("Reproduced the published test precision (45.2% and 52.0%); nothing was tuned.\n")

print(f"1. Where the threshold rule placed each model (mode {MODE}; test base rate {100 * y.mean():.1f}%)")
print("   rule: among thresholds with validation precision >= 60%, take the one with the highest recall\n")
print("   model            threshold | validation: precision  recall  says yes | test: precision  recall  says yes | PR-AUC validation -> test")
for name, thr, p in (("LightGBM", thr_lgbm, p_lgbm), ("duration curve", thr_curve, p_curve)):
    v, t = VAL[name], got[name]
    print(f"   {name:15s}  {thr:8.3f} | {v[0]:21.1f} {v[1]:7.1f} {v[2]:9.1f} | {t[0]:15.1f} {t[1]:7.1f} {t[2]:9.1f} | {VAL_PR_AUC[name]:.1f} -> {100 * average_precision_score(y, p):.1f}")

print("\n2. The two answers at the same selectiveness on the test")
print("   LightGBM's threshold is moved so that it says yes exactly as often as the duration curve does.")
print("   This uses the forecasts only, not the outcomes, so it is not a tuned result - but it is not the frozen program either.\n")
curve_yes = p_curve >= thr_curve
k = int(curve_yes.sum())
matched = np.zeros(len(y), bool)
matched[np.argsort(-p_lgbm, kind="stable")[:k]] = True
for name, pred in (("duration curve, frozen threshold", curve_yes), ("LightGBM, same share of yes", matched), ("LightGBM, frozen threshold", p_lgbm >= thr_lgbm)):
    a, b, c = stats(pred)
    print(f"   {name:34s} precision {a:5.1f}%   endings caught {b:5.1f}%   says yes {c:5.1f}%")

local = X.index[test].tz_convert(KYIV_TZ) - pd.Timedelta(hours=12)
block = pd.factorize(local.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))[0]
nb = block.max() + 1
picks = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, nb, (2000, nb))


def boot(pred):
    tp = np.bincount(block, weights=pred & y, minlength=nb)[picks].sum(axis=1)
    return tp / np.bincount(block, weights=pred, minlength=nb)[picks].sum(axis=1)


d = 100 * (boot(matched) - boot(curve_yes))
print(f"   LightGBM at the same share of yes minus duration curve: {stats(matched)[0] - stats(curve_yes)[0]:+.1f} points, 95% interval {np.percentile(d, 2.5):+.1f} .. {np.percentile(d, 97.5):+.1f} (day-block bootstrap, 2,000 draws)")

print("\n3. LightGBM's precision along its own curve on the test (the price of being permissive)")
order = np.argsort(-p_lgbm, kind="stable")
hits = np.cumsum(y[order])
for share in (0.10, 0.25, 0.49, 0.68, 0.88, 1.00):
    n = max(int(round(share * len(y))), 1)
    print(f"   says yes for the top {share:4.0%} of moments: precision {100 * hits[n - 1] / n:5.1f}%   endings caught {100 * hits[n - 1] / y.sum():5.1f}%")

print("\n4. Did the probabilities shift? (mean forecast against observed frequency, test)")
for name, p, thr in (("LightGBM", p_lgbm, thr_lgbm), ("duration curve", p_curve, thr_curve)):
    print(f"   {name:15s} mean forecast {100 * p.mean():.1f}%, observed {100 * y.mean():.1f}%; share of moments above its threshold {100 * (p >= thr).mean():.1f}% (validation: {VAL[name][2]:.1f}%)")

print("\n5. What LightGBM leans on, and whether it still means the same")
imp = joblib.load(ROOT / "models" / f"lgbm_end_{FNAME}.joblib").importance().head(6)
print("   top features of the final model: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.1%}" for k, v in imp.items()))
periods = {"train": train, "validation": val, "test": test}
print("\n   during a Kyiv alert, by period:        " + "".join(f"{n:>12s}" for n in periods))
rows = {
    "alert ends within 30 min, %": lambda m: 100 * Y["y_end"][m].mean(),
    "Chernihiv under alert, %": lambda m: 100 * X["chernihiv_on"][m].mean(),
    "Chernihiv: newest alert < 30 min old, %": lambda m: 100 * (X["chernihiv_newest_min"][m] < 30).mean(),
    "Poltava under alert, %": lambda m: 100 * X["poltava_on"][m].mean(),
    "Kyiv alert already lasts > 60 min, %": lambda m: 100 * (X["kyiv_on_min"][m] > 60).mean(),
}
for label, fn in rows.items():
    print(f"   {label:39s}" + "".join(f"{fn(m):12.1f}" for m in periods.values()))

print("\n   chance that the Kyiv alert ends within 30 min, by how recently a new alert started in Chernihiv oblast:")
print("   Chernihiv's newest alert              " + "".join(f"{n:>12s}" for n in periods) + "   (share of test moments)")
bands = [("no alert in Chernihiv", lambda v: v.isna()), ("started < 30 min ago", lambda v: v < 30), ("30-90 min ago", lambda v: (v >= 30) & (v < 90)),
         ("90-180 min ago", lambda v: (v >= 90) & (v < 180)), ("180 min ago or more", lambda v: v >= 180)]
for label, cond in bands:
    cells, share = [], 0.0
    for name, m in periods.items():
        sel = cond(X["chernihiv_newest_min"][m])
        cells.append(f"{100 * Y['y_end'][m][sel].mean():12.1f}" if sel.sum() >= 30 else f"{'-':>12s}")
        if name == "test":
            share = 100 * sel.mean()
    print(f"   {label:39s}" + "".join(cells) + f"   {share:6.1f}%")

print("\n   the same for the duration curve's only input, how long the Kyiv alert has lasted:")
print("   Kyiv alert has lasted                 " + "".join(f"{n:>12s}" for n in periods) + "   (share of test moments)")
for label, lo, hi in (("< 15 min", 0, 15), ("15-30 min", 15, 30), ("30-60 min", 30, 60), ("60-120 min", 60, 120), ("> 120 min", 120, 1e9)):
    cells, share = [], 0.0
    for name, m in periods.items():
        v = X["kyiv_on_min"][m]
        sel = (v >= lo) & (v < hi)
        cells.append(f"{100 * Y['y_end'][m][sel].mean():12.1f}")
        if name == "test":
            share = 100 * sel.mean()
    print(f"   {label:39s}" + "".join(cells) + f"   {share:6.1f}%")

content.text:
Обґрунтування є, і воно спирається на виміри: LightGBM не гірша модель — гіршою виявилась точка, у яку наше правило порога поставило його відповідь. Нічого не перенавчав і не змінював: LightGBM завантажено зі збереженого файлу, програма та сама.

## Причина: три ланки

**1. Правило порога поставило дві моделі в дуже різні точки.** Правило з рішення 21: серед порогів із точністю ≥ 60% на валідації взяти той, що ловить найбільше закінчень. LightGBM ранжував на валідації значно краще, тому міг дозволити собі набагато поблажливіший поріг і все одно показати там 60%.

| | Поріг | Валідація: точність / каже «так» | Тест: точність / каже «так» |
|---|---|---|---|
| LightGBM | 0,223 | 60,0% / 68% | 45,2% / 88% |
| Крива тривалості | 0,393 | 60,7% / 54% | 52,0% / 49% |

Тобто правило винагородило кращий валідаційний результат порогом, близьким до «завжди так». Відповідь, що каже «так» 88% часу, не може бути помітно точнішою за базову частоту 41%, якою б не була модель.

**2. На тесті ймовірності LightGBM виявились завищеними.** Середній прогноз 54,8% проти 41,1% фактичних. Через це частка моментів над порогом зросла з 68% до 88%. У кривої тривалості навпаки: 37,2% проти 41,1%, частка над порогом 54% → 49%.

**3. Закономірність, яку вивчив LightGBM, перестала діяти.** Його головні ознаки — як давно почалась нова тривога в Чернігівській і Полтавській (30% внеску моделі разом). Шанс, що київська тривога закінчиться за 30 хв:

| Ситуація | Навчання | Валідація | Тест |
|---|---|---|---|
| У Чернігівській немає тривоги | 66,9% | 71,3% | 27,4% |
| Нова тривога в Чернігівській почалась < 30 хв тому | 79,5% | 71,3% | 54,3% |
| Київська тривога триває < 15 хв (вхід кривої) | 51,8% | 61,4% | 54,6% |
| Київська тривога триває > 120 хв (вхід кривої) | 18,6% | 26,0% | 22,8% |

У навчанні й валідації «в Чернігівській тихо» означало швидкий відбій у 67–71% випадків, на тесті — у 27%. Модель і далі давала в цих ситуаціях високу ймовірність. Єдиний вхід кривої тривалості лишився майже стабільним.

## Головний контрольний замір

Якщо зсунути поріг LightGBM так, щоб він казав «так» рівно так само часто, як крива (49% часу тривоги), його точність 50,6% проти 52,0%. Різниця −1,4 пункта, 95% інтервал −12,1 … +9,2 — моделі не відрізняються. Для цього зсуву потрібні лише прогнози, без відповідей, тож це не підгонка; але це й не та програма, яку ми заморозили.

Точність LightGBM уздовж його власної кривої на тесті: 65% для найвпевненіших 10% моментів, 55% для 25%, 50% для 49%, 45% для 88%.

## Чого це не доводить

- **Чому змінилась закономірність із Чернігівською** — не досліджував. Клітинки малі: рядок «немає тривоги» — це 11% із 1 915 моментів, тобто кілька десятків тривог одного незвично інтенсивного літа.
- **Що інше правило було б кращим.** Правило «фіксована частка так» замість «максимум повноти» тут виявилось би стійкішим, але це знання заднім числом: воно не було узгоджене і не перевірене на невикористаних даних. У README так і записано.

- [scripts/end_diagnostics.py](scripts/end_diagnostics.py) і [reports/end_diagnostics_output.txt](reports/end_diagnostics_output.txt). Скрипт перевіряє, що відтворює опубліковані 45,2% і 52,0%, і зупиняється, якщо ні.
